title: S2-RL: Sample-Set Dual Reinforcement Learning for Generative Semantic Segmentation Dataset Distillation

paper.title: S 2 -RL: Sample-Set Dual Reinforcement Learning for Generative Semantic Segmentation Dataset Distillation
paper.abstract:
Abstract While dataset distillation has witnessed significant advances in image classification, its extension to dense prediction tasks such as semantic segmentation is plagued by two core bottlenecks: bi-level optimization-based approaches suffer from prohibitive computational costs stemming from pixel-wise gradient unrolling, whereas proxy-based generative methods merely infuse visual textures into fixed semantic masks derived from real data, thus failing to condense rich semantic knowledge into a compact set of informative, novel scene generations.
To address both bottlenecks simultaneously, we propose a novel Sample-Set Reinforcement Learning (S 2 -RL) framework for generative semantic segmentation dataset distillation (SSDD). Specifically, S 2 -RL formulates SSDD as a diffusion model based text-to-image generation paradigm, enabling flexible generation of images with informative, novel semantic distributions via a concise text prompt. Furthermore, we fine-tune a diffusion policy via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), leveraging a sample-set dual reward
paradigm: for individual samples, it enforces semantic alignment with input text prompts and intra-class feature diversity; for sample sets, it maximizes inter-sample semantic distribution diversity by solving a contextual multi-armed bandit problem. These design choices enable S 2 -RL to distill large-scale semantic segmentation datasets into a compact set of generated samples that encapsulate diverse, informative semantic knowledge without the need of pixel-wise gradient unrolling.
Extensive experiments on the ADE20K and COCO datasets demonstrate that S 2 -RL achieves substantial and consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, establishing a new benchmark for SSDD.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Data-efficient learning has become crucial as deep learning models grow increasingly data-hungry. Dataset distillation [ 40 ] addresses this by condensing massive datasets into compact synthetic surrogates. Existing advances in dataset distillation fall into two primary paradigms: optimization-based methods and proxy-based generative methods. While both paradigms yield strong performance on image classification, their extension to dense prediction tasks such as semantic segmentation remains fraught with substantial challenges. Specifically, optimization-based methods (Figure 1(a) ), such as gradient matching [ 48 , 3 , 50 ] and distribution matching [ 39 , 49 , 28 ] , formulate dataset distillation as a bi-level optimization problem aiming to align the gradients or distributions of student models on synthetic data with those on the real counterpart. While theoretically rigorous, these methods suffer from computational intractability in semantic segmentation tasks. Unlike image classification, which only relies on sparse supervision, semantic segmentation requires unrolling pixel-wise gradients at full spatial resolution, leading to severe memory overhead and making end-to-end optimization practically infeasible. To circumvent this memory bottleneck, proxy-based generative methods [ 45 , 35 ] (Figure 1(b) ) have emerged as an efficient alternative, which bypass bi-level optimization via data inversion or global statistic matching. Since global statistics matching cannot comprehensively depict the complex spatial arrangements of multiple categories, existing approaches, such as those for object detection [ 27 ] or universal dataset distillation [ 26 ] , turn to rely on fixed spatial masks from real data for structural regularization. This strategy reduces the model to a mere texture filler within static boundaries, rather than a genuine scene composer, and thus fails to synthesize a compact set of novel, informative spatial layouts necessary for covering the long-tail distributions of real-world scenes. To bridge these gaps, we propose a novel S ample- S et R einforcement L earning (S 2 -RL) framework for generative semantic segmentation dataset distillation (SSDD), as shown in Figure 1(c) . Unlike existing gradient-heavy or mask-conditioned methods, we reformulate SSDD as a diffusion-based text-to-image generation paradigm and optimize it through reward-driven reinforcement learning without pixel-wise gradient unrolling through downstream segmentation training. By framing the generative model as an agent, S 2 -RL directly utilizes appropriate rewards to drive policy updates. This framework not only eliminates the need for heavy second-order gradient computations, but also empowers the model to flexibly synthesize a compact set of images with novel, informative contents from concise text prompts, thus enabling effective SSDD. However, applying RL to generative dataset distillation introduces a new challenge. Standard RL methods (e.g., DDPO [ 2 ] , Flow-GRPO [ 21 , 38 ] ) are typically designed for sample-level optimization, aiming to maximize the quality of individual instances. In contrast, dataset distillation is fundamentally a set-level optimization problem: the objective is to construct a collective dataset that covers the original dataset distribution with fewer samples. Straightforwardly applying standard RL is prone to incur model collapse, where the model over-optimizes for easy patterns while ignoring the long-tail distribution characteristics of real datasets. To address this problem, we introduce a sample-set dual reward mechanism. At the sample-level, for each individual generated sample, we enforce semantic alignment with the input prompt while penalizing collapsed local textures within the same class. At the set-level, we maximize inter-sample semantic distribution diversity by solving a contextual multi-armed bandit problem, enabling the generated compact sample set to appropriately cover the original long-tail dataset distribution. Empirical evaluations on ADE20K [ 51 ] and COCO [ 20 ] benchmarks demonstrate that S 2 -RL outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reconciling generation quality with distributional diversity. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose S 2 -RL, a novel generative dataset distillation framework that leverages RL to enable efficient image synthesis for dense prediction tasks, bypassing the memory bottlenecks of explicit gradient matching. • We design a dual reward mechanism that balances sample quality and set diversity, mitigating semantic mode collapse. • We obtain new state-of-the-art SSDD performance on ADE20K and COCO datasets.

sections.heading: 2.1 Data-Efficient Learning
sections.text: Coreset Selection. This paradigm selects a representative subset from the original data. Classical methods include random selection, which samples data stochastically, and uniform selection, which ensures balanced sampling across categories. Beyond these, geometry-based methods leverage feature space structures. Herding [ 41 , 6 ] selects samples closest to the cluster center of each class to approximate the mean of the distribution. Conversely, K-Center [ 11 , 30 ] aims to minimize the maximum distance between any data point and the selected subset, effectively prioritizing boundary samples to maximize geometric coverage. While efficient, these extraction-based methods are inherently bounded by the finite samples available in the source domain, limiting their ability to bridge distributional gaps through synthesis. Optimization-based Dataset Distillation. To synthesize informative data, early methods formulated dataset distillation as a bi-level optimization problem. Gradient matching methods [ 48 , 3 , 50 ] align the gradients or long-term training dynamics of student and teacher models, while distribution matching methods [ 39 , 49 , 28 ] optimize distribution or feature statistics. Differentiable augmentation [ 47 ] , neural feature regression [ 52 ] , and difficulty-aligned trajectory matching [ 14 ] further advance classification distillation. Extending such methods to high-resolution dense prediction remains challenging. In particular, approaches that differentiate through student training face prohibitive memory costs when unrolling pixel-wise computation graphs. Proxy-based Generative Dataset Distillation. To bypass the heavy optimization, recent works have shifted towards proxy-based generative methods. Model inversion methods [ 45 , 9 , 32 ] invert pretrained model statistics (e.g., BatchNorm) to recover training images. Generative attempts [ 35 , 4 , 53 ] leverage the rich priors of generative models to synthesize diverse data distributions by matching global statistics or embedding alignments. Minimax Diffusion [ 13 ] additionally balances representativeness and diversity during generative training. However, a critical gap remains when transferring these successes to semantic segmentation. Due to the lack of spatial location information in global statistics, existing methods, such as those for object detection [ 27 ] or universal distillation [ 26 ] , typically require pre-defined layouts from real data to constrain the generation process. This dependency limits the synthesized dataset to the topological variations already in the training set, hindering the exploration of novel scene layouts. Unlike optimization methods that face computational barriers, or proxy methods that depend on static mask priors, S 2 -RL adopts a reward-driven policy optimization paradigm. This allows for the autonomous construction of complex scene topologies without unrolling downstream student-training gradients or using fixed masks as generation conditions.

sections.heading: 2.2 Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Models
sections.text: Reinforcement Learning has recently been integrated with diffusion models to align generation with specific objectives. DDPO [ 2 ] treats the multi-step denoising process as a policy, enabling the optimization of non-differentiable reward functions via policy gradient. DPO-Diffusion [ 37 ] simplifies this by leveraging preference pairs to optimize the policy without an explicit reward model. To further enhance training stability, Flow-GRPO [ 21 , 38 ] estimates gradients using the relative advantage of sampled groups, eliminating the need for a separate value network. While these methods have successfully improved sample quality, they primarily focus on sample-level optimization. In the context of dataset distillation, our S 2 -RL extends these frameworks to a set-level perspective, utilizing RL not just for individual image quality, but to actively explore and cover the diverse semantic distribution required for robust downstream training.

sections.heading: 4.1 Framework Overview
sections.text: As illustrated in Figure , S 2 -RL reformulates SSDD as an RL-based generation process. We fine-tune a pretrained Stable Diffusion policy π θ \pi_{\theta} to synthesize a dataset 𝒟 s ​ y ​ n \mathcal{D}_{syn} that maximizes downstream semantic segmentation performance. In each iteration, the agent samples a text prompt c c and synthesizes an image x ^ \hat{x} . To optimize this generative process without accessing prohibitive pixel-wise gradients, we employ GRPO to update the policy parameters θ \theta , directly maximizing a total reward signal R t ​ o ​ t ​ a ​ l R_{total} based on the feedback from the synthesized samples. The efficacy of this optimization relies on our proposed sample-set dual reward mechanism, which evaluates the generation at two distinct granularities. Class-list prompts specify category presence and co-occurrence while leaving spatial arrangements to the generator. In the following sections, we detail how R s ​ a ​ m ​ p ​ l ​ e R_{sample} and R s ​ e ​ t R_{set} are formulated to steer the policy toward high-fidelity and diverse synthesis.

sections.text: To guide the policy update, we integrate the proposed hierarchical rewards into a unified feedback signal. The total reward R t ​ o ​ t ​ a ​ l R_{total} for a generated image x ^ \hat{x} conditioned on prompt c c is computed as a weighted summation: R t ​ o ​ t ​ a ​ l ​ ( x ^ , c ) = γ a ​ R a ​ l ​ i ​ g ​ n ​ ( x ^ , c ) + γ d ​ R d ​ i ​ v ​ ( x ^ ) + γ s ​ R s ​ e ​ t ​ ( x ^ , c ) , R_{total}(\hat{x},c)=\gamma_{a}R_{align}(\hat{x},c)+\gamma_{d}R_{div}(\hat{x})+\gamma_{s}R_{set}(\hat{x},c), (8) where γ a , γ d , γ s \gamma_{a},\gamma_{d},\gamma_{s} are hyperparameters balancing semantic alignment, within-class diversity, and prototype coverage. We optimize the diffusion policy π θ \pi_{\theta} using Eq. 3 . Optimization Behavior. The combined reward objective biases the policy toward prompt-consistent, feature-diverse, and semantically well-covered samples, discouraging degenerate solutions by jointly leveraging sample-level quality rewards and a set-level coverage reward. We refer readers to Proposition 5 in Appendix A for a detailed interpretation.

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Settings
sections.text: Datasets and Metrics. We evaluate our framework on two challenging benchmarks: ADE20K [ 51 ] and COCO [ 20 ] . For COCO, we utilize the panoptic annotations converted into semantic segmentation masks to ensure high-quality pixel-wise supervision. As one of the first systematic studies of dataset distillation specifically tailored to semantic segmentation, we establish a standardized evaluation protocol adapted from the image classification task’s images per class (IPC) metric; specifically, considering the multi-class nature of segmentation images, we determine the data budget based on global compression ratios rather than fixed class counts. Accordingly, we set the ratios to 0.25%, 0.5%, 1.0% for ADE20K and 0.625‰, 1.25‰, 2.5‰ for the larger COCO dataset to align with standard distillation scales (e.g., 10/20/50 IPC). We report mean intersection over union (mIoU) and mean pixel accuracy (mAcc) as the primary metrics. For the main comparisons, we construct 5 dataset groups and train 5 student seeds per group, reporting mean and standard deviation over the 25 downstream runs. Baselines. We compare S 2 -RL with two categories of baselines: (1) coreset selection methods: We include Random selection, Uniform sampling (class-balanced), K-Center [ 11 , 30 ] , and Herding [ 41 , 6 ] . We employ a pretrained ResNet-50 [ 15 ] to extract deep features for distance computation in K-Center and Herding. (2) generative baselines: Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium (SD3.5) [ 10 ] serves as our vanilla generative baseline, and UniDD ∗ [ 26 ] denotes our reproduced UniDD-inspired proxy-guided segmentation baseline. Implementation details of UniDD ∗ are provided in Appendix B.2 . Implementation Details. (1) RL and Set Construction: We employ Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium [ 10 ] as the policy backbone, fine-tuned via LoRA [ 17 ] with a rank of 32. To construct the text conditioning, we utilize the image subset selected by the Uniform baseline. Specifically, we extract all category names present in each selected image and concatenate them into a comma-separated string (e.g., “person, car, tree”) to serve as the multi-category prompt. The policy is optimized using AdamW [ 24 ] at learning rate 1e-4. After policy adaptation, we generate candidate images and screen them using the same sample-level and set-level reward functions used in training. A pretrained teacher model then supplies pixel-wise pseudo-labels for the retained images. (2) Evaluation Stage: We independently train a student on each synthesized dataset using MMSegmentation [ 8 ] . Our default student is SegFormer-B5 [ 43 ] , whose MiT-B5 backbone is initialized from ImageNet-1K-pretrained weights for each run. The models are trained for 200 epochs using the AdamW optimizer with a crop size of 512 × 512 512\times 512 . Additional architectural variations are detailed in the ablation studies.

We assess data quality with the complex-scene examples in Figure 3 . While the SD3.5 baseline generates texturally plausible images, it often omits objects requested in dense prompts, such as specific furniture in Row 4 or distinct vehicles in Row 2. In contrast, S 2 -RL synthesizes scenes with higher semantic density, retaining richer structure and detail, from the foliage in Row 1 to the cluttered interior decor in Row 4. Such multi-category scenes provide supervision for several semantic regions and their shared context within each training image. This is valuable for dense prediction, where the student learns object appearance together with its surrounding scene structure. Preserving requested objects also retains boundaries between semantic regions, providing supervision for class transitions alongside region appearance. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: We propose S 2 -RL, a generative framework for semantic segmentation dataset distillation that fine-tunes Stable Diffusion via GRPO with a sample-set dual reward, integrating sample-level fidelity and set-level coverage to bypass the computational bottlenecks of bi-level optimization and the static-prior limitation of proxy-based methods. Experiments on ADE20K and COCO show consistent state-of-the-art gains, and our RL-driven paradigm offers a scalable path toward distillation for broader dense-prediction tasks. The framework incurs an upfront policy-adaptation cost and depends on pretrained generative and segmentation priors. Its rewards approximate downstream utility, and pseudo-labels may inherit teacher errors on rare or ambiguous categories. Future work could reduce adaptation and sampling costs, improve pseudo-label reliability through uncertainty-aware annotation, and incorporate lightweight student feedback to better align reward optimization with segmentation performance without full gradient unrolling.

sections.heading: Appendix B Detailed Implementation Settings
sections.text: In this section, we provide the comprehensive hyperparameter settings and architectural details required to reproduce our experiments. Our framework is implemented using PyTorch and the Diffusers library [ 36 ] based on GRPO Guard [ 38 ] .

sections.heading: B.1 Architecture Details
sections.text: Policy Model. We utilize Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium [ 10 ] as our backbone policy π θ \pi_{\theta} . To ensure training efficiency and prevent catastrophic forgetting of the pretrained generative priors, we adopt low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [ 17 ] for fine-tuning. • Base Model: Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium (2.5B parameters). • LoRA Configuration: We inject LoRA layers into the attention mechanisms of the MMDiT. The LoRA rank is set to 32, with an alpha value of 64. • Trainable Parameters: Only the LoRA weights ( ∼ \sim 70 MB) are updated during the RL phase. Reward Models. Our dual-reward mechanism relies on three types of frozen pretrained models, each playing a distinct role: • Semantic Evaluator Ensemble. For ADE20K we use UPerNet-ConvNeXt-Large [ 42 , 23 ] , SegFormer-B5 [ 43 ] , and DPT-Large [ 29 ] ; for COCO we use Mask2Former-Swin-Large [ 7 ] , EOMT-Large [ 19 ] , and EOMT-Base. Each frozen evaluator computes alignment from its own mask and diversity from its own intermediate feature grid, using at most 100 locations per predicted class. We sum the resulting scalar sample rewards. Raw feature vectors from different architectures are never compared. Per-pixel majority voting combines the masks only for DINOv3 region pooling in the set-level reward. • Pseudo-Label Teacher. The downstream student is trained on synthesized images paired with pseudo-labels produced by a single, stronger frozen segmentor: UPerNet-ConvNeXt-XLarge for ADE20K and Mask2Former-Swin-Large for COCO. The same teacher is used to label images from all synthetic baselines (SD3.5, UniDD ∗ , and S 2 -RL), so the annotation procedure and downstream training protocol are shared across methods. • Feature Extractor. The set-level reward (Eq. 7 ) is computed on dense patch features from a frozen DINOv3 ViT-L model [ 33 ] . The semantic mask from the segmentor ensemble is downsampled by nearest-neighbor interpolation to match the DINOv3 patch grid, and DINOv3 features are L 2 -normalized along the channel dimension before any cosine-similarity computation. DINOv3 is used only for semantic-arm construction and matching in R s ​ e ​ t R_{set} .

sections.heading: B.2 UniDD-inspired Proxy-guided Baseline
sections.text: We implement a UniDD-inspired proxy-guided baseline as an additional generative comparison. UniDD [ 26 ] uses task-specific proxy models to extract task-relevant supervision and guide diffusion-based dataset distillation. Since the official UniDD implementation is not publicly available, we implement a segmentation-oriented proxy-guided baseline using a released pretrained FreestyleNet [ 44 ] checkpoint as the layout-to-image generator, while following the proxy-guided sampling and refinement principle of UniDD. This implementation corresponds to the UniDD ∗ entries in Table and Table 1 . The proxy-guided baseline initializes generation from the masks selected by the Uniform baseline. This keeps the layout source and compression budget aligned with the real-data subset baselines, while replacing the corresponding real images with generated images. FreestyleNet takes dense semantic layouts as conditions and synthesizes images aligned with the input masks, making it suitable for adapting proxy-guided generation to semantic segmentation. The proxy segmentation model is dataset-specific. For ADE20K, we use SegFormer-B0 as the proxy segmentation model. For COCO, we use MaskFormer-R50 as the proxy segmentation model. During generation, the proxy model scores the semantic consistency between the generated image and the input mask, and this score is used for refinement and filtering. After image generation, we use the same pseudo-labeling teacher as S 2 -RL to obtain pixel-wise annotations, so that all synthetic baselines are evaluated with the same downstream training pipeline. We follow the original UniDD hyperparameter setting as closely as possible. Each image is generated with 250 sampling steps. The filtering threshold is set to 0.75. A generated image is accepted if its proxy score exceeds this threshold. If the proxy score remains below the threshold for three consecutive attempts, we keep the highest-scoring image among the attempted samples. This fallback rule preserves a fixed dataset size for every compression ratio and prevents failed generations from changing the number of downstream training images. We report this method as UniDD ∗ to indicate that it is a segmentation-oriented adaptation of UniDD rather than the official implementation. Compared with the vanilla SD3.5 baseline, UniDD ∗ uses mask-conditioned generation and task-specific proxy filtering. Compared with S 2 -RL, it does not fine-tune the diffusion policy with sample-set rewards, but instead relies on iterative proxy-guided sampling from the pretrained FreestyleNet generator.

sections.heading: Zero-KL setting.
sections.text: We use the zero-KL setting adopted in the GRPO-Guard [ 38 ] training configuration, where the KL loss is not applied. GRPO-Guard stabilizes GRPO-style optimization for diffusion/flow models through regulated clipping, implemented by ratio normalization and gradient reweighting across denoising timesteps. These operations restore more balanced importance-ratio distributions and reduce timestep-wise gradient imbalance during policy optimization.

sections.heading: B.4 GRPO Reward Computation Details
sections.text: We describe the reward computation process used during GRPO fine-tuning. In each training iteration, we sample 16 text prompts from the prompt pool. For each prompt, the rollout policy generates a group of 8 trajectories for ADE20K or 16 for COCO, each producing one candidate image. Rewards are computed on the final images, while the policy update uses the stored denoising trajectories to evaluate the clipped per-step importance-ratio objective described in Appendix A.1 . For each generated image, we compute the sample-level reward terms, including semantic alignment and intra-class feature diversity. The semantic alignment reward evaluates whether the generated image is consistent with the target semantic content specified by the prompt. The intra-class diversity reward evaluates whether the image contains discriminative class-level features rather than repetitive or collapsed visual patterns. These two terms are computed independently for each image and provide local supervision for sample quality. The set-level reward is computed on the same generated batch rather than on a separate reward batch. After extracting semantic features from all generated images in the current iteration, each feature is assigned to its nearest semantic prototype. We then accumulate the prototype-count increment induced by the current mini-batch. The set-level reward is evaluated using both the historical prototype counts and the current batch-level increment, before committing the new counts to the global memory. This batch-aware update prevents reward inflation across iterations rather than within a single batch: samples that match the same prototype within a single iteration receive the same exploration bonus, but historical counts are updated only after the entire batch has been evaluated, so later iterations correctly see the marginal coverage contributed by the previous one. After combining the sample-level and set-level rewards, GRPO computes advantages within each same-prompt group. Specifically, the G G rewards belonging to one prompt are normalized within that group, and the resulting advantages are clipped to [ − 5 , 5 ] [-5,5] before use in the surrogate. We do not normalize rewards across all 16 prompts in the iteration. This design ensures that the policy compares alternative generations under the same semantic condition, rather than mixing reward scales across unrelated prompts. The sample-level and set-level rewards serve different roles in optimization. The sample-level rewards guide each individual image toward semantic correctness and feature discriminability. The set-level reward tracks prototype visitation during policy training and assigns larger bonuses to under-covered semantic modes. Therefore, the set-level reward does not duplicate the sample-level objectives; instead, it introduces a dataset-level exploration signal that encourages the policy to construct a more balanced and informative synthetic set.

sections.heading: E.1 Protocol and Metric Definitions
sections.text: We evaluate five stored constructed sets per method at ADE20K 1.0% (202 images per set) and COCO 2.5‰ (295 images per set). A frozen OneFormer-Swin-L [ 18 ] annotates both the constructed images and the official held-out validation reference (2,000 ADE20K and 5,000 COCO images). All four methods, including real-image Uniform selection, use this same annotation source. OneFormer was unused by the original reward, candidate-selection, pseudo-labeling, and student-training pipelines for these sets. This diagnostic is therefore independent of the reward evaluator, although it still relies on pretrained dataset priors. For semantic appearance, we mask-pool ImageNet-1K V2 ResNet-50 layer-4 features extracted at 448 × 448 448\times 448 resolution; this feature extractor is also unused by the reward. We discard class regions smaller than 0.1% of image area and repeat the analysis at 0.2%. The OneFormer checkpoint revisions are fixed to 4a5bac8e64f82681a12db2e151a4c2f4ce6092b2 (ADE20K) and 3a263017ca5c75adbea145f25f81b118243d4394 (COCO). Local-support coverage and precision (C/P). For a held-out descriptor, its self-excluded real 5-nearest-neighbor distance defines a fixed support radius. Coverage is the fraction of held-out descriptors with a constructed descriptor inside their support ball; precision is the fraction of constructed descriptors supported by the union of these fixed real-reference balls. Feature C/P applies this rule to mask-pooled ResNet features, and occupancy C/P to normalized 4 × 4 4\times 4 class-occupancy descriptors. Both are macro-averaged over reference-eligible classes. These are local-support diagnostics, distinct from standard generative precision/recall. Pair recall/precision and geometry C/P. Pair recall and precision compare the unique category pairs co-occurring within images. For each category pair, geometry uses one descriptor per image from the two class-union masks: horizontal and vertical centroid displacement, log area ratio, and centroid distance normalized by the image diagonal. Geometry C/P applies the fixed-reference support rule separately to pairs with at least ten held-out observations and macro-averages over eligible pairs. These descriptors measure pairwise spatial support, not object boundaries, higher-order scene graphs, or full topology. We also report class-conditional Vendi [ 12 ] on the pooled ResNet features. Statistical scope. Tables 14 and 15 give means and sample standard deviations across five stored sets. A content-hash check found no constructed/reference or cross-method image overlap, but images can be reused across sets of the same method. The reported variation is descriptive set-level variation, not independent-policy uncertainty or a significance test.

sections.heading: Appendix F Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: While S 2 -RL establishes a new state-of-the-art for semantic segmentation dataset distillation, we identify several limitations inherent to the current framework and outline promising directions for future research.

sections.heading: F.1 Limitations
sections.text: Dataset Construction Cost. S 2 -RL incurs an upfront policy-adaptation cost of approximately 48 GPU-hours, followed by multi-step diffusion sampling. Selection-based methods are substantially cheaper to construct. Although policy optimization avoids differentiating through dense student-training updates, the intended use is offline extreme compression with repeated reuse of a constructed set; the measured generative budget does not establish an end-to-end lifecycle speedup. Dependency on pretrained Priors. Our framework relies on the rich semantic priors encapsulated in the pretrained Stable Diffusion 3.5 and the frozen segmentor reward model. Consequently, the performance of S 2 -RL is bounded by the capabilities of these foundation models. For extremely rare categories not well-represented in the Stable Diffusion training corpus, the policy may struggle to generate high-fidelity textures even with RL fine-tuning. Pseudo-Label Fidelity. Generated training masks can inherit teacher errors, especially for small or ambiguous regions. Reward Proxy Gap. We utilize a frozen segmentor as a proxy to estimate the downstream utility of generated samples. While effective, this is an approximation of the true student learning dynamics. There exists a theoretical gap between maximizing the frozen segmentor’s confidence and minimizing the student’s validation loss. In rare cases, the agent might learn to hack the reward by generating adversarial features that satisfy the frozen segmentor but are less transferable to a student model trained independently on the constructed dataset.

sections.heading: F.2 Future Work
sections.text: Extension to Other Dense Prediction Tasks. The proposed sample-set dual reward paradigm is generic and not limited to semantic segmentation. Future work could extend S 2 -RL to other dense prediction tasks, such as instance segmentation by incorporating box-level alignment rewards and depth estimation by replacing the semantic evaluator with a depth consistency reward. Student-in-the-Loop Optimization. To bridge the reward proxy gap mentioned above, future iterations could incorporate feedback directly from the student model being trained. Although calculating gradients through the student involves high memory costs (the original bi-level bottleneck), one could employ meta-learning techniques or periodic reward model updates to approximate the student’s needs without full gradient unrolling.

sections.heading: Appendix G Broader Impacts
sections.text: This work studies semantic segmentation dataset distillation under compact data budgets. Its primary positive impact is improving the efficiency of dense prediction research by reducing the number of annotated training samples required for downstream model development. By constructing compact synthetic training sets, S 2 -RL may lower storage, annotation, and iteration costs for semantic segmentation experiments, which can make dense prediction model development more accessible in resource-constrained settings. The method also inherits several limitations and risks from pretrained generative and segmentation models. Since S 2 -RL relies on pretrained text-to-image generators and frozen reward evaluators, the generated samples may reflect biases, artifacts, or category imbalances present in these models or in the original training datasets. If such distilled sets are used without careful validation, downstream models may inherit these biases or perform unevenly across rare or visually ambiguous categories. Therefore, the generated data should be treated as a compact training surrogate for research evaluation rather than as a replacement for carefully curated real annotations in safety-critical applications. Affiliation: Northwestern Polytechnical University Wei Wei Affiliation: Northwestern Polytechnical University Chen Ding Affiliation: Xi’an University of Posts & Telecommunications https://github.com/00why00/S2RL Abstract While dataset distillation has witnessed significant advances in image classification, its extension to dense prediction tasks such as semantic segmentation is plagued by two core bottlenecks: bi-level optimization-based approaches suffer from prohibitive computational costs stemming from pixel-wise gradient unrolling, whereas proxy-based generative methods merely infuse visual textures into fixed semantic masks derived from real data, thus failing to condense rich semantic knowledge into a compact set of informative, novel scene generations. To address both bottlenecks simultaneously, we propose a novel Sample-Set Reinforcement Learning (S 2 -RL) framework for generative semantic segmentation dataset distillation (SSDD). Specifically, S 2 -RL formulates SSDD as a diffusion model based text-to-image generation paradigm, enabling flexible generation of images with informative, novel semantic distributions via a concise text prompt. Furthermore, we fine-tune a diffusion policy via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), leveraging a sample-set dual reward paradigm: for individual samples, it enforces semantic alignment with input text prompts and intra-class feature diversity; for sample sets, it maximizes inter-sample semantic distribution diversity by solving a contextual multi-armed bandit problem. These design choices enable S 2 -RL to distill large-scale semantic segmentation datasets into a compact set of generated samples that encapsulate diverse, informative semantic knowledge without the need of pixel-wise gradient unrolling. Extensive experiments on the ADE20K and COCO datasets demonstrate that S 2 -RL achieves substantial and consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, establishing a new benchmark for SSDD. (a) Optimization-based methods (b) Proxy-based methods (c) S 2 -RL (Ours) Figure 1 : Comparison of paradigms. (Left) Optimization-based methods incur prohibitive memory costs from unrolling pixel-wise gradients. (Middle) Proxy-based generative methods require masks from real data, restricting synthesized datasets to existing layouts. (Right) S 2 -RL treats distillation as active scene construction, using RL to generate diverse spatial topologies and valid scene layouts from text alone. 1 Introduction Data-efficient learning has become crucial as deep learning models grow increasingly data-hungry. Dataset distillation [ 40 ] addresses this by condensing massive datasets into compact synthetic surrogates. Existing advances in dataset distillation fall into two primary paradigms: optimization-based methods and proxy-based generative methods. While both paradigms yield strong performance on image classification, their extension to dense prediction tasks such as semantic segmentation remains fraught with substantial challenges. Specifically, optimization-based methods (Figure 1(a) ), such as gradient matching [ 48 , 3 , 50 ] and distribution matching [ 39 , 49 , 28 ] , formulate dataset distillation as a bi-level optimization problem aiming to align the gradients or distributions of student models on synthetic data with those on the real counterpart. While theoretically rigorous, these methods suffer from computational intractability in semantic segmentation tasks. Unlike image classification, which only relies on sparse supervision, semantic segmentation requires unrolling pixel-wise gradients at full spatial resolution, leading to severe memory overhead and making end-to-end optimization practically infeasible. To circumvent this memory bottleneck, proxy-based generative methods [ 45 , 35 ] (Figure 1(b) ) have emerged as an efficient alternative, which bypass bi-level optimization via data inversion or global statistic matching. Since global statistics matching cannot comprehensively depict the complex spatial arrangements of multiple categories, existing approaches, such as those for object detection [ 27 ] or universal dataset distillation [ 26 ] , turn to rely on fixed spatial masks from real data for structural regularization. This strategy reduces the model to a mere texture filler within static boundaries, rather than a genuine scene composer, and thus fails to synthesize a compact set of novel, informative spatial layouts necessary for covering the long-tail distributions of real-world scenes. To bridge these gaps, we propose a novel S ample- S et R einforcement L earning (S 2 -RL) framework for generative semantic segmentation dataset distillation (SSDD), as shown in Figure 1(c) . Unlike existing gradient-heavy or mask-conditioned methods, we reformulate SSDD as a diffusion-based text-to-image generation paradigm and optimize it through reward-driven reinforcement learning without pixel-wise gradient unrolling through downstream segmentation training. By framing the generative model as an agent, S 2 -RL directly utilizes appropriate rewards to drive policy updates. This framework not only eliminates the need for heavy second-order gradient computations, but also empowers the model to flexibly synthesize a compact set of images with novel, informative contents from concise text prompts, thus enabling effective SSDD. However, applying RL to generative dataset distillation introduces a new challenge. Standard RL methods (e.g., DDPO [ 2 ] , Flow-GRPO [ 21 , 38 ] ) are typically designed for sample-level optimization, aiming to maximize the quality of individual instances. In contrast, dataset distillation is fundamentally a set-level optimization problem: the objective is to construct a collective dataset that covers the original dataset distribution with fewer samples. Straightforwardly applying standard RL is prone to incur model collapse, where the model over-optimizes for easy patterns while ignoring the long-tail distribution characteristics of real datasets. To address this problem, we introduce a sample-set dual reward mechanism. At the sample-level, for each individual generated sample, we enforce semantic alignment with the input prompt while penalizing collapsed local textures within the same class. At the set-level, we maximize inter-sample semantic distribution diversity by solving a contextual multi-armed bandit problem, enabling the generated compact sample set to appropriately cover the original long-tail dataset distribution. Empirical evaluations on ADE20K [ 51 ] and COCO [ 20 ] benchmarks demonstrate that S 2 -RL outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reconciling generation quality with distributional diversity. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose S 2 -RL, a novel generative dataset distillation framework that leverages RL to enable efficient image synthesis for dense prediction tasks, bypassing the memory bottlenecks of explicit gradient matching. • We design a dual reward mechanism that balances sample quality and set diversity, mitigating semantic mode collapse. • We obtain new state-of-the-art SSDD performance on ADE20K and COCO datasets. 2 Related Work 2.1 Data-Efficient Learning Coreset Selection. This paradigm selects a representative subset from the original data. Classical methods include random selection, which samples data stochastically, and uniform selection, which ensures balanced sampling across categories. Beyond these, geometry-based methods leverage feature space structures. Herding [ 41 , 6 ] selects samples closest to the cluster center of each class to approximate the mean of the distribution. Conversely, K-Center [ 11 , 30 ] aims to minimize the maximum distance between any data point and the selected subset, effectively prioritizing boundary samples to maximize geometric coverage. While efficient, these extraction-based methods are inherently bounded by the finite samples available in the source domain, limiting their ability to bridge distributional gaps through synthesis. Optimization-based Dataset Distillation. To synthesize informative data, early methods formulated dataset distillation as a bi-level optimization problem. Gradient matching methods [ 48 , 3 , 50 ] align the gradients or long-term training dynamics of student and teacher models, while distribution matching methods [ 39 , 49 , 28 ] optimize distribution or feature statistics. Differentiable augmentation [ 47 ] , neural feature regression [ 52 ] , and difficulty-aligned trajectory matching [ 14 ] further advance classification distillation. Extending such methods to high-resolution dense prediction remains challenging. In particular, approaches that differentiate through student training face prohibitive memory costs when unrolling pixel-wise computation graphs. Proxy-based Generative Dataset Distillation. To bypass the heavy optimization, recent works have shifted towards proxy-based generative methods. Model inversion methods [ 45 , 9 , 32 ] invert pretrained model statistics (e.g., BatchNorm) to recover training images. Generative attempts [ 35 , 4 , 53 ] leverage the rich priors of generative models to synthesize diverse data distributions by matching global statistics or embedding alignments. Minimax Diffusion [ 13 ] additionally balances representativeness and diversity during generative training. However, a critical gap remains when transferring these successes to semantic segmentation. Due to the lack of spatial location information in global statistics, existing methods, such as those for object detection [ 27 ] or universal distillation [ 26 ] , typically require pre-defined layouts from real data to constrain the generation process. This dependency limits the synthesized dataset to the topological variations already in the training set, hindering the exploration of novel scene layouts. Unlike optimization methods that face computational barriers, or proxy methods that depend on static mask priors, S 2 -RL adopts a reward-driven policy optimization paradigm. This allows for the autonomous construction of complex scene topologies without unrolling downstream student-training gradients or using fixed masks as generation conditions. 2.2 Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Models Reinforcement Learning has recently been integrated with diffusion models to align generation with specific objectives. DDPO [ 2 ] treats the multi-step denoising process as a policy, enabling the optimization of non-differentiable reward functions via policy gradient. DPO-Diffusion [ 37 ] simplifies this by leveraging preference pairs to optimize the policy without an explicit reward model. To further enhance training stability, Flow-GRPO [ 21 , 38 ] estimates gradients using the relative advantage of sampled groups, eliminating the need for a separate value network. While these methods have successfully improved sample quality, they primarily focus on sample-level optimization. In the context of dataset distillation, our S 2 -RL extends these frameworks to a set-level perspective, utilizing RL not just for individual image quality, but to actively explore and cover the diverse semantic distribution required for robust downstream training. 3 Preliminaries 3.1 Problem Formulation Semantic Segmentation Dataset Distillation. In each iteration, the agent samples a text prompt c c and synthesizes an image x ^ \hat{x} . We evaluate our framework on two challenging benchmarks: ADE20K [ 51 ] and COCO [ 20 ] . For COCO, we utilize the panoptic annotations converted into semantic segmentation masks to ensure high-quality pixel-wise supervision. As one of the first systematic studies of dataset distillation specifically tailored to semantic segmentation, we establish a standardized evaluation protocol adapted from the image classification task’s images per class (IPC) metric; specifically, considering the multi-class nature of segmentation images, we determine the data budget based on global compression ratios rather than fixed class counts. Accordingly, we set the ratios to 0.25%, 0.5%, 1.0% for ADE20K and 0.625‰, 1.25‰, 2.5‰ for the larger COCO dataset to align with standard distillation scales (e.g., 10/20/50 IPC). We report mean intersection over union (mIoU) and mean pixel accuracy (mAcc) as the primary metrics. For the main comparisons, we construct 5 dataset groups and train 5 student seeds per group, reporting mean and standard deviation over the 25 downstream runs. Baselines. We compare S 2 -RL with two categories of baselines: (1) coreset selection methods: We include Random selection, Uniform sampling (class-balanced), K-Center [ 11 , 30 ] , and Herding [ 41 , 6 ] . We employ a pretrained ResNet-50 [ 15 ] to extract deep features for distance computation in K-Center and Herding. (2) generative baselines: Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium (SD3.5) [ 10 ] serves as our vanilla generative baseline, and UniDD ∗ [ 26 ] denotes our reproduced UniDD-inspired proxy-guided segmentation baseline. Implementation details of UniDD ∗ are provided in Appendix B.2 . Implementation Details. (1) RL and Set Construction: We employ Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium [ 10 ] as the policy backbone, fine-tuned via LoRA [ 17 ] with a rank of 32. To construct the text conditioning, we utilize the image subset selected by the Uniform baseline. Specifically, we extract all category names present in each selected image and concatenate them into a comma-separated string (e.g., “person, car, tree”) to serve as the multi-category prompt. The policy is optimized using AdamW [ 24 ] at learning rate 1e-4. After policy adaptation, we generate candidate images and screen them using the same sample-level and set-level reward functions used in training. A pretrained teacher model then supplies pixel-wise pseudo-labels for the retained images. (2) Evaluation Stage: We independently train a student on each synthesized dataset using MMSegmentation [ 8 ] . Our default student is SegFormer-B5 [ 43 ] , whose MiT-B5 backbone is initialized from ImageNet-1K-pretrained weights for each run. The models are trained for 200 epochs using the AdamW optimizer with a crop size of 512 × 512 512\times 512 .
